extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of formal logic / philosophy (learners of syllogistic logic and theory of inference)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and constructing valid syllogisms and distinguishing induction from ratiocination; explicating the structural and substantive principles that make reasoning (inference) legitimate or informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper inference (distinct conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inference (reasoning properly so called) is one in which we set out from known truths to arrive at others really distinct from them; exclude cases where the logical consequent is a mere repetition of the antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count as reasoning those progressions where the conclusion merely repeats what the premise already asserts. The page contrasts mere verbal repetition with true inference and excludes tautological transitions from the province of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction versus Ratiocination (definition by generality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is inferring a proposition from propositions less general than itself (conclusion more general than premises); Ratiocination (syllogism) is inferring a proposition from propositions equally or more general (conclusion equally or less general).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to classify arguments: when conclusion is more general than largest premise call it induction; when it is equally or less general call it ratiocination. The same structural process (combining premises to derive a broader generalization) is treated as induction when the result is more general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of a legitimate syllogism (three propositions and three terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate syllogism requires exactly three propositions (two premises + conclusion) and exactly three terms: the minor (subject of conclusion), the major (predicate of conclusion), and the middle term which appears in both premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure no more than three propositions/terms are used; identify major/minor premises correctly (major premise contains middle and major term; minor premise contains middle and minor term). Examples: 'All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of syllogism (position of middle term)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogisms are classified into figures (first to fourth) according to whether the middle term is subject in both premises, predicate in both, subject in one and predicate in the other, etc.; most common is first figure (middle subject of major, predicate of minor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which figure an argument is in by locating the middle term. Note that some logicians use three figures (folding fourth into first); Lambert and others analyze which arguments fit each figure more naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moods (quantity and quality of propositions) and legitimate moods
rubrics_metrics.description: Each figure is divided into moods according to quantity (universal or particular) and quality (affirmative or negative). Only certain combinations (listed in the text) are legitimate where the conclusion necessarily follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the enumerated legitimate mood-figure combinations (examples provided for all legitimate moods in first through fourth figures). Treat singular propositions as universals for syllogistic purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion and reduction rules (reduce to first figure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any valid ratiocination in figures 2–4 may be reduced to an equivalent syllogism in the first figure by converting one or both premises (simple conversion for universal negatives; conversion per accidens for universal affirmatives into particulars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conversion rules to transform premises (e.g., No C is B → No B is C). Use conversion per accidens to change All B is A into Some A is B when necessary. Reduction shows all valid ratiocination can be expressed in first-figure forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of singular propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular propositions are ranked with universal propositions in syllogistic reasoning because their predicate is affirmed or denied of the whole of the subject (e.g., 'Socrates is a man' treated like a universal affirmative for purposes of syllogism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building syllogisms, consider singulars as universals so they fit the standard moods and figures; examples in text illustrate this equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictum de omni et nullo (critique of as sole foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim 'whatever can be affirmed (or denied) of a class may be affirmed (or denied) of every thing included in the class' (dictum de omni et nullo) is inadequate as an explanatory principle of ratiocination when universals are treated as mere names rather than real entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on dictum de omni as a substantive grounding of inference when propositions convey factual relations rather than mere classificatory conventions. The text argues the maxim is trivial (often merely tautological) unless supplemented by an account of propositions as assertions about facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions as factual assertions (not merely classificatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A real proposition asserts a matter of fact dependent on laws of nature (attributes co-existing or not), not merely the meaning of words; this factual content is essential to the logical value of syllogisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate premises for factual content: check that premises assert real relations of attributes (co-existence/incompatibility) rather than merely naming conventions. This grounds ratiocination in facts rather than verbal manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental axioms underlying syllogism (affirmative and negative co-existence principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principles underlie all non-verbal syllogisms: (1) Affirmative: things which co-exist with the same thing co-exist with one another (transitivity of co-existence). (2) Negative: if a thing co-exists with another which does not co-exist with a third, then the first does not co-exist with the third (incompatibility transference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these axioms to test whether an argument's probative force depends on factual relations. The text treats them as axioms akin to mathematical axioms and as the real ground of syllogistic legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism reformulated as 'marks' (practical formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every syllogism can be expressed practically as: 'Attribute A is a mark of attribute B; the given object has mark A; therefore the given object has attribute B.' This restates general propositions as evidential marks for practical inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt this phrasing to clarify the practical/explanatory role of premises. The axioms correspondingly read: 'Whatever has any mark has that which it is a mark of,' or 'Whatever is a mark of any mark is a mark of that which the latter is a mark of.' Examples in text show how classical syllogisms map to this formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: petitio principii and apparent newness of conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every syllogism contains a petitio principii in that nothing in the conclusion is really outside what is presupposed in the premises; yet a syllogism may present to a reasoner a conclusion that feels like a new truth because it unfolds what was implicitly contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating arguments, check for hidden premises or implicit assumptions: a syllogism cannot produce information not already involved in premises, though it can reveal implicit content. This distinction is crucial in assessing the epistemic role of syllogistic reasoning (e.g., knowing the Duke of Wellington is mortal via general principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of general premises in ratiocination (major premise universal)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the canonical first-figure forms presented, the major premise is universal (affirmative or negative) and the other premise is affirmative; this structure drives whether the conclusion is affirmative or negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure syllogisms so that the major premise affirms/denies an attribute of an entire class and the minor premise affirms inclusion of the subject; then derive the appropriate affirmative/negative conclusion. Text gives canonical templates for proving affirmatives and negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal affirmative conclusions require first figure
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions that are universal affirmatives (the most important scientific class) are susceptible of proof in the first figure alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming to prove a universal affirmative, ensure argument is or reducible to first-figure form; other figures cannot prove universal affirmative conclusions.
